title: DNS translation and NAT affinity playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for private deployments (VPC + on-prem) focusing on deterministic DNS translation and NAT session affinity. The objective is to document practical patterns and a minimal Terraform module interface to support:
- consistent name resolution across split-horizon and cross-site scenarios
- stable NAT behavior for long-lived websocket/streaming sessions
- migration steps for customers upgrading from basic NAT gateway setups to an affinity-capable, policy-aware egress layer

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to Redwood Private deployments where the customer runs a VPC or on-prem cluster and wants to route outbound traffic through a managed egress layer (Redwood-managed appliances or customer Reverse NAT box).
- Assumes we can deploy CoreDNS or equivalent in the control plane (ConfigMap sync ok) and that we can provision trunked subnets, floating IPs, and route-table entries via Terraform and on-prem runbooks.
- Does NOT cover: enterprise BGP peering design, deep IPS/IDS policies, or application-layer proxies (beyond simple HTTP/TCP passthrough).

Topology sketch (ASCII):

  customer-vpc                  redwood-egress-subnet           internet
  +------------+               +-------------------+         +---------+
  | k8s nodes  |--(pod ip)---> |  egress-proxy     | --NAT--->| origin  |
  | (10.10.x.x) |               |  (10.200.0.10)    |         | servers |
  +------------+               +-------------------+         +---------+
        |                             ^  |
        |                             |  +-- DNS forwarding to CoreDNS
        +-- Node-local DNS (stub) ----+

Key patterns and rationale:
1) DNS translation table (operator-controlled)
   - Use CoreDNS with a git-backed ConfigMap for per-customer split-horizon entries. Keep a small translation table with host->target mappings for on-prem reachable hostnames and for private endpoints that must resolve to internal IPs when on the private network.
   - Benefits: predictable resolution, easier to support service migrations (we can rotate target IPs without exposing public mapping).
   - Risk: drift between customer DNS policies and our table. Add a quick audit script to detect mismatches (see tests).

2) Hairpin NAT for on-host service loopback
   - Some deployments require pod->cluster service->egress->public IP->back to cluster path. Enable hairpin NAT on the egress box (or use iptables MASQUERADE rules) when hairpin_enabled is true in Terraform.
   - Prefer explicit hairpin rules vs universal SNAT to avoid masquerading internal-only flows.

3) Session affinity for streaming / websocket workloads
   - Problem: standard nat gateway SNAT randomizes source port and can map new outbound ports across a pool; long-lived connections on subsequent reconnections may land on different egress addresses, causing backend session break.
   - Solution: implement hash-based source-port selection and/or conntrack pinning for sessions matching criteria (protocol websocket/http2, or by JWT cookie). Options:
     a) Conntrack stickiness using connmark + iptables --set-xmark on first egress and restore for subsequent packets.
     b) eBPF-based redirect that preserves 5-tuple mapping consistently across restarts.
   - Tradeoff: connmark approach is easier to implement but needs careful conntrack tuning. eBPF has lower latency but is more operationally complex.

4) Per-tenant egress policies (connmark + routing table)
   - Use connmark to tag flows by tenant at the NAT-forwarding layer, then use ip rule / ip route to select different SNAT addresses or exit peers. This avoids NAT table explosion and isolates quotas.

Terraform module sketch (module: private-egress)
Variables (recommended):
  - name (string)
  - vpc_id (string)
  - egress_subnet_ids (list(string))
  - dns_forwarders (list(string))  # upstream resolver IPs for external queries
  - internal_translation_map (list(string)) # small list of host=ip entries, or path to S3/secret containing mapping
  - hairpin_enabled (bool)
  - affinity_mode (string) # none | conntrack | ebpf
  - conntrack_max (number)   # conntrack table target
  - nat_pool (list(string))  # list of floating IPs to use for SNAT
  - enable_connmark (bool)
  - monitoring_hooks (map)   # simple string list of endpoints to push metrics to

Outputs (recommended):
  - nat_ips (list(string))
  - route_table_ids (list(string))
  - coredns_configmap_name (string)
  - affinity_mode (string)
  - conntrack_status_endpoint (string)

Example usage (HCL fragment):
  module "private_egress" {
    source = "github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules//private-egress"
    name = "acme-nyc-egress"
    vpc_id = aws_vpc.cluster.id
    egress_subnet_ids = [aws_subnet.egress1.id, aws_subnet.egress2.id]
    dns_forwarders = ["10.10.0.2", "10.10.0.3"]
    internal_translation_map = ["meta.internal=10.100.5.12"]
    hairpin_enabled = true
    affinity_mode = "conntrack"
    conntrack_max = 524288
    nat_pool = [aws_eip.nat1.public_ip, aws_eip.nat2.public_ip]
  }

Upgrade and migration plan (phases):
Phase 0 - discovery and gating (1-3 days)
  - Inventory current NAT devices and mapping (collect current conntrack_max, conntrack entries, current SNAT IPs).
  - Run DNS audit: compare authoritative customer DNS vs proposed translation map.
  - Stakeholders: customer SRE, Redwood solutions engineer.

Phase 1 - pilot (1 week)
  - Deploy module in pilot VPC with hairpin disabled, affinity_mode=none. Verify egress and DNS forwarding.
  - Smoke tests: wget/curl to public endpoints, websocket reconnect tests, TLS handshake checks.
  - Verify CoreDNS overrides for internal names.

Phase 2 - enable affinity + conntrack tuning (2-7 days)
  - flip affinity_mode to conntrack in pilot and watch conntrack table growth. Raise conntrack_max as needed and adjust nf_conntrack UDP/TCP timeouts for idle detection.
  - Add healthcheck for conntrack saturation.

Phase 3 - staged rollout (2-4 weeks)
  - Roll out per-customer, small batches. Provide fallback to original NAT gateway using route-table switch or policy-based routing.
  - Monitor: successful websocket reconnect rate, TLS renegotiation counts, downstream 5xx rates.

Rollback strategy:
  - Route-table revert to previous NAT gateway (fast) or remove SNAT rules and re-apply customer's original gateway config.
  - If conntrack saturation occurs, immediately reduce affinity_mode to none and revert NAT pool.

Verification and runbooks (quick checks):
  - DNS: dig @<cluster-dns> service.internal +short => expected internal ip
  - Egress IP check: curl --interface <node-ip> https://ifconfig.me => should return one of nat_pool IPs
  - Hairpin: curl to service DNS that resolves to public ip from pod -> should resolve and reach local service (no routing loop)
  - Conntrack: ss -s | grep "estab" and sudo conntrack -L | grep <ip> to validate sticky entries

Monitoring and alerting:
  - Metrics to collect: conntrack_total, conntrack_rate, nat_errors, dns_forward_errors, egress_rtt_p50/p90, websocket_reconnect_rate.
  - Alerts: conntrack > 80% of conntrack_max for 5m, dns_forward_errors > 1% for 10m, websocket_reconnect_rate > baseline by 10%

Operational notes & tuning knobs (practical tips):
  - Kernel knobs: net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max, net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established, vm.max_map_count for iptables modules. Document per-instance recommended values in module README.
  - If using AWS NAT Gateway replacement: consider AWS TGW/route table switch to minimize route flap scope.
  - For on-prem: test with iptables-legacy vs nft for conntrack behavior—nft may have different default timeouts.
  - Keep a small downstream DNS TTL (30s) for translation entries during migration windows so we can rotate IPs quickly.

Open questions / TODOs:
  - Decide default affinity_mode for new customers (conntrack vs none). Recommend conntrack for streaming-heavy customers.
  - Provide an automated test harness that simulates 10k websocket connections to measure conntrack growth and reconnection behavior. (JIRA-3456)
  - Explore eBPF proof-of-concept for lower-latency affinity (track with PR #89).
  - Make internal_translation_map representation pluggable (list vs S3 vs KV store).

Appendix: Quick troubleshooting checklist (first 15 mins)
 1) Check CoreDNS configmap in cluster: kubectl -n kube-system get configmap coredns -o yaml | grep -A3 "meta.internal"
 2) Check routes: ip route show table main and ip rule list
 3) Verify NAT IPs: iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v | grep MASQUERADE or nft list table nat
 4) Conntrack saturation: sudo cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count and nf_conntrack_max
 5) Reproduce and capture: tcpdump -i <egress-if> host <backend-ip> and kubectl logs egress-proxy

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep the module API tiny; we can add complexity later.
- Operator-friendly defaults: affinity_mode=none, hairpin_enabled=false, conntrack_max=131072.
- Need to coordinate docs with solutions-engineering runbooks in Confluence.

End of draft.

Small TODOs in-file:
